correctness.rationale: For \(K_{n_1,\ldots,n_r}\), each neighborhood is the complement of one part. The two-color equations force exact balance in every part, hence all part sizes even. The two four-vertex obstructions are proved directly. For \(N\ge12\), a consecutive-block periodic three-coloring leaves every outside-part color triple with spread at most two; neighborhoods of size at least six then satisfy the half bound, while the sole possible low-degree largest part is placed last and checked from its balanced initial segment. Every smaller profile is exhausted by part-by-color count matrices, which are a complete quotient of vertex colorings for this graph class. The packaged verifier rechecks the finite closure and construction tests.

originality.rationale: The 2026 defining paper covers cycles and complete graphs but not complete multipartite graphs. The exact two-color branch is explicitly credited to the 2024 neighborhood-balanced theorem, so it is not treated as novel. Targeted searches and inspection of the closest 2026 balance and game papers found no theorem giving the exact static strong-majority number for arbitrary complete multipartite profiles or identifying \(K_{2,1,1}\) as the only additional four-color obstruction.
residual_risks: An older or poorly indexed theorem under a different local-balance terminology could conceivably imply the three-color construction, although searches explicitly included neighborhood-balanced and lambda-balanced aliases.
The exact two-color branch and complete-graph subfamily are known prior results; originality rests on the residual arbitrary-multipartite three-versus-four classification.

value.rationale: Strong majority coloring is a newly introduced local coloring parameter whose behavior is unbounded in general. Complete multipartite graphs are a canonical dense family on which the exact parameter was not given by the defining paper. The result closes the whole family with a sharp parity threshold and exactly two four-color exceptions, while separating previously known two-color neighborhood balance from the genuinely new three-color regime. This is a natural complete classification rather than an arbitrary finite slice.
